analysis.one_liner: Cuts federal aid to college programs whose graduates can't actually get licensed in their field.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 2 Democratic cosponsors, never received a committee vote or floor vote and died in the Senate HELP Committee when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred colleges from federal student aid for any program that prepares students for a licensed occupation — like nursing or plumbing — unless finishing the program actually qualifies students to sit for the required licensing exam and get licensed where they live or where the school advertises. Schools would also have to arrange required clinical placements, internships, or apprenticeships on time. For newer, not-yet-accredited programs, the Education Department would have to write rules requiring schools to sign agreements to discharge students' loans if the program fails them.
analysis.who_benefits: Students enrolling in programs that promise to lead to a licensed job — especially veterans and low-income students whose federal aid and loans flow to these programs. They would gain a guarantee that the program qualifies them for licensure in their own area, timely clinical or internship placements, and loan discharge if a school's unaccredited program leaves them with a useless credential.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Students in licensed-trade and health programs

how_it_helps.text: Programs preparing students for licensed occupations would lose access to federal aid — including Title IV student aid, workforce funding, and military and veterans' education benefits — unless completing the program fully qualifies students for the required licensing exam and certification in the state and metro area where they live, and in any state the school advertises.
Schools would have to provide timely placement in required pre-licensure steps such as clinical placements, internships, or apprenticeships, rather than leaving students stuck waiting for slots.

The Education Department would have to write rules holding pre-accredited programs to the same consumer protections and requiring schools to sign a loan discharge agreement with each enrolled student.

analysis.who_pays: Colleges — particularly for-profit career schools — running occupational programs that cannot currently get their graduates licensed would have to fix the programs, restrict their advertising claims, or give up federal aid. Some schools might drop or shrink programs rather than bear the cost of clinical placements and state-by-state compliance.

drawbacks.text: Schools would have had only one year to meet the requirements or lose federal aid for affected programs [S2]. A short compliance deadline could lead some schools to close occupational programs instead of fixing them, reducing access to training in some areas.

Requiring programs to qualify students for licensure in every state and metro area where they advertise is demanding; a school could reasonably argue that licensing rules vary by state and that students sometimes fail exams for reasons the school cannot control.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections are targeted at a real, well-documented problem — federal aid and loans flowing to programs whose graduates cannot obtain the license the program promised to prepare them for. The cost falls on schools that would have to redesign programs, arrange placements, or curb advertising, and a one-year deadline raised a genuine risk of program closures. On balance the bill put the risk of a worthless credential on the school rather than the student, which is why the protections were limited to licensed-occupation programs.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in September 2014 and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never took it up before the Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Sen. Jeff Merkley introduced the bill on September 18, 2014, with Sen. Tom Harkin, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
The action history shows no further action — no committee markup, no floor vote — before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.
Two Democratic senators cosponsored the bill, and no version passed either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Schools offering occupational programs that do not lead to licensure keep federal aid without these consumer protections, and the risk of unpaid loans and worthless credentials stays with students. The for-profit college sector, which opposed this type of regulation, avoided new requirements.

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Protecting Students from Worthless Degrees Act and referred it to the HELP Committee.

for.name: Sen. Tom Harkin
for.role: U.S. Senator (IA), cosponsor; Chairman of the Senate HELP Committee
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, but his committee never scheduled a markup or vote on it.

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no markup, no vote — and it died at the end of the Congress.

against.name: For-profit college industry
against.role: Sector most affected by the bill
against.what_they_did: Actively opposed similar Obama-era consumer-protection rules for career college programs during this period.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the sponsor and both cosponsors were Democrats, and the bill received no recorded Republican support or opposition.

industries.note: These schools earn most of their revenue from federal student aid and veterans' benefits, and many occupational programs have been criticized for leaving graduates unable to get licensed. The bill would cut off federal aid unless programs actually qualify students for licensure and arrange required placements, so the sector loses revenue unless it redesigns programs.

industries.industry: Colleges and universities offering licensed-occupation programs (nonprofit and public)
industries.note: Well-run programs that already place students in clinicals and get them licensed face little change and gain a guardrail against weaker competitors. Schools with advertising that overstates where graduates can work would have to change it or lose aid.
